beats.say: You hear the clatter of swords as Shinpūren samurai storm the Kumamoto barracks in January 1876.
Their secret oath forbade any weapon forged after the Meiji Restoration, a radical vow few understood.
They believed the imperial army's new rifles were cursed spirits stealing Japan's ancient soul.
Leader Miyoshi Shigeyoshi, a former low-rank artilleryman, turned his own gun into a wooden replica for ritual.
On February 24, they launched a midnight raid, killing 30 conscripts and sparking panic across Kyushu.
The government's response was swift: General Nogi Maresuke ordered a siege, surrounding the rebels with artillery.
Inside the cramped temple hideout, the Shinpūren sang an ancient chant, believing it would summon kami.
When the walls finally fell, only five survived, each swearing to die before bowing to Western guns.
Their defeat became a cautionary tale, yet the rebels inspired later ultranationalist movements in the 1930s.
History remembers the Shinpūren not for victory, but for their fierce refusal to surrender tradition.
